meta.purpose: RAG knowledge base for the Resume-JD Matcher
meta.problem_statement: PS section 6: ~50 short chunks (<500 chars each), sourced from publicly available resume-writing guides and industry skill checklists (NTU Career & Attachment Office public materials, O*NET skill lists or equivalent).
meta.change_note: v1 was 51 chunks written for this project as a paraphrase of the sources named in the PS. v2 replaces it with material actually harvested from named public platforms: O*NET 31.0 occupation profiles (US Department of Labor / ETA, CC BY 4.0), ESCO skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0) and published CV/ATS guidance read from live web sources. Reason: v1's chunks were prose-paraphrase with heavy shared boilerplate, so a lexical retriever could not separate relevant from irrelevant chunks (calibration separation +0.0429, 15/20 queries saturated the scale).
meta.provenance: No copyrighted text is reproduced. O*NET technology and skill NAMES are quoted as short factual labels from a CC BY database; ESCO labels are quoted likewise. Prose in every chunk is written for this project. Each chunk records a `source` so retrieval provenance stays auditable in every run log.

licences.CV/ATS guidance: paraphrased from public vendor blogs; no text reproduced

constraints.privacy: Contains no personal data and no real candidate information.

meta.maintenance: Edit this file, then run: python -m data.knowledge_base.build_kb. Re-run scripts/calibrate_similarity.py whenever this file changes - the similarity scale is fitted to this corpus.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: A skills list on an application is specific to ONE posting, not a permanent inventory. Cross-reference your own skills against that job description and keep only the ones the posting names or clearly implies through its responsibilities; discard the rest for this application. The same candidate applying to two different roles should present two different lists.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Order a skills list by relevance to the role being applied for, not by personal pride or by how strong the skill is in the abstract. A resume skills line usually carries eight to twelve items; a short application form field carries two or three. Selecting the strongest personal skill when the posting does not ask for it wastes the slot.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Mirror the posting's own vocabulary. Applicant tracking systems match on literal terms, so 'stakeholder management' and 'managing stakeholders' are not interchangeable to a ranking algorithm even when they describe the same work. Where the posting repeats a phrase, that repetition is the employer telling you which requirement matters most.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Give both the acronym and its expansion once: RAG (retrieval augmented generation), ETL (extract, transform, load), NPR (natural language processing). Some systems index the short form, others the long one, and the safest option is to carry both in the same phrase rather than choosing.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Keep a skill in a list only if it also appears somewhere else in the document as evidence. A skills line with no supporting bullet is an unverifiable claim; interviewers routinely probe the first two items, so a run of unsupported entries converts a strong application into a credibility problem.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: When a stated requirement is genuinely missing from the candidate's evidence, do not manufacture it and do not list it anyway. Either leave it out, or state the closest adjacent thing precisely and let the reader judge the transfer. Keyword-stuffing an unheld skill is the single most damaging mistake in a tailored application.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Adjacent evidence can legitimately count toward a requirement. A statistics course supports model evaluation; a report where the candidate chose the metric supports analytics; a deployed side project supports engineering. Name the specific activity and what it produced, not the label: 'built the evaluation harness' maps to model evaluation, 'worked on AI' maps to nothing.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Most large employers parse the document with an applicant tracking system before a human reads it. Plain single-column layout, standard headings ('Skills', 'Experience', 'Education'), and no text inside images, icons or text boxes are the practical rules. Two-column templates and decorative layouts routinely reorder content into nonsense during parsing.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Group a long skills list into two or three labelled lines - languages, then frameworks and tools, then domain skills - instead of one undifferentiated wall. Grouping is easier for a parser to segment and easier for a reader to scan, and it stops unrelated entries from reading as padding. A single flat list of thirty items is the pattern that gets filtered.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Compress each accomplishment to one line using Situation, Action, Result. Lead with a verb, name the skill used, and close on the outcome. The result is what the reader looks for first; a bullet with an action but no result reads as a job description rather than as an accomplishment, and carries almost no screening weight.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Lead every bullet with a concrete verb - built, automated, migrated, reduced, designed, measured, shipped, debugged. Avoid 'responsible for', 'helped with', 'involved in' and 'assisted', which describe proximity to work rather than contribution. A hiring manager cannot score proximity, and these phrases are the most common filler in graduate documents.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Quantify where you honestly can: percent faster, items processed, users served, hours saved, error rate, budget managed. With no measurement available, quantify scope instead - team size, dataset size, number of releases, duration, number of stakeholders. A real count beats an invented percentage, and an invented percentage is a fabrication risk.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: The contact block needs a professional email address, a mobile number, and optionally a portfolio or profile URL. It does not need a full mailing address, date of birth or photograph. Keep the name in the plainest form the candidate actually uses, since the same string is copied into the employer's application form.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: An education entry is institution, degree or programme, major, and expected graduation month and year. If a GPA is stated, name the scale - a 4.2 without saying it is out of 5.0 tells the reader nothing. Use the institution's full official name rather than an abbreviation, because the form field and the parser both expect the full string.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: A summary is two or three lines and names the role being targeted plus the three capabilities most relevant to it. Rewriting the summary is the highest-leverage thirty-second change available per application. Bulk-sent objectives copied across postings actively weaken a document, because they signal that nothing was read.

chunks.source: Published CV/ATS guidance (paraphrase)
chunks.text: Before submitting, check four things: the file is a PDF named with the candidate's own name, the contact details are current, every date is internally consistent, and the same role title does not appear twice. Then read it aloud once - sentences that are hard to say are usually also hard to read.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Data Scientists (O*NET-SOC 15-2051.00) develop and implement techniques and analytics applications that turn raw data into usable information: data mining, data modelling, machine learning and natural language processing over large structured and unstructured datasets, then interpreting and reporting the findings. Typical tasks include evaluating model performance, documenting method and limitations, and communicating results to non-specialists.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: AI and machine learning core vocabulary: Python; machine learning; supervised learning; unsupervised learning; deep learning and neural networks; feature engineering; model evaluation including cross-validation and held-out test sets; and the ability to critique a model's error analysis rather than only its headline accuracy. Statistical literacy underpins all of it.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: AI/ML tooling named in O*NET's technology-skill records for data scientists: PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, IBM SPSS, SAS, The MathWorks MATLAB, and Apache Spark. Day-to-day data manipulation is pandas and NumPy. Saying which framework was used for which task, and why, counts for more than listing all of them; Hugging Face and the transformers library cover pretrained model work.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 + ESCO skill definitions (CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Text and language stack: natural language processing (NLP), tokenisation, text classification, transformer-based models, and evaluation with precision, recall and F1 rather than accuracy alone. LLM-adjacent work adds large language models (LLM), prompt engineering, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over a private document set, and vector database concepts such as embedding similarity search.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Machine learning operations (MLOps) covers everything between a trained model and a service another team can call: model deployment and model serving, containerisation with Docker, orchestration with Kubernetes, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) for model code, version control with Git for notebooks as well as source, and monitoring to detect drift. It also means reproducibility - a container image anyone can rebuild.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: The data layer under AI work: SQL with joins, aggregations and window functions; pandas and NumPy for manipulation; data cleaning, which O*NET records as the largest single share of the job; and enough judgement to sanity-check a table before modelling on it. A candidate who can describe a data quality problem they found, and what they did about it, reads as more senior than one who only lists modelling techniques.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Data Scientists 15-2051.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Adjacent experience that legitimately supports an AI or machine learning application: statistics coursework, which maps to model evaluation; any data pipeline built end to end, which maps to feature engineering and cleaning; and any project where something was deployed for other people to use, which maps to MLOps. State the specific activity and its outcome rather than the label.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Software Developers (O*NET-SOC 15-1252.00) design, build and maintain applications and services. O*NET lists the essential skills as critical thinking, active learning, reading comprehension, active listening, writing, speaking and monitoring - the technical stack sits on top of those. Representative tasks: analyse requirements, write and test code, review others' changes, and diagnose failures in systems already running.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: General-purpose languages in O*NET's software-skill records for software developers: Python, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, C#, C++, Go, Scala and R, plus Bash and shell scripting on Linux and UNIX. The expectation for a graduate is depth in at least one language at a level where unfamiliar code can be debugged, not shallow familiarity with several.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Service and interface design: REST APIs and RESTful API conventions, HTTP status codes, authentication headers, JSON payloads, GraphQL where it is used, and input validation at the boundary. Microservices versus a modular monolith, synchronous versus event-driven calls, idempotency and caching are the vocabulary interviews probe. Being able to describe how a failing third-party API was handled is the reliability answer interviewers want.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Testing expectations: unit testing of pure logic, integration testing across a boundary, and reproducing a bug as a failing test before fixing it. O*NET records JUnit, Selenium, LoadRunner and SonarQube among the tools for this occupation. Naming a framework matters less than being able to describe one test that actually caught a regression.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Delivery and operations tooling recorded for software developers: Docker for reproducible environments; Kubernetes, Red Hat OpenShift and Terraform for orchestration; Jenkins CI, GitLab, GitHub and Bitbucket for continuous integration and version control; Prometheus, Grafana and Splunk for observability. For a graduate, having configured a CI workflow that ran tests and blocked a bad merge is strong, concrete evidence.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Most software roles touch a database. Expected knowledge: schema basics, indexing intuition, transactions, and SQL that goes beyond a bare SELECT. PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Redis, DynamoDB and Oracle appear in the technology records for this occupation. Being able to explain why a query was slow and what was changed is a common practical interview question for backend-leaning graduate roles.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Software Developers 15-1252.00 + 13-1082.00 (CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Process vocabulary: Agile, Scrum, Kanban, sprint planning, and issue tracking in Atlassian Jira with documentation in Confluence. Also expected: writing a clear pull-request description, reviewing another person's code without ego, version control etiquette in Git, and estimating honestly. Agile appears in nearly every posting, so naming a specific ceremony contributed to is more credible than listing the framework.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Business Intelligence Analysts (O*NET-SOC 15-2051.01) turn data into information that supports a decision: querying warehouses, building reports and dashboards, and interpreting results for the people who act on them. O*NET lists the essential skills as reading comprehension, active learning, active listening, critical thinking, speaking, writing, mathematics and monitoring - communication carries as much weight as the tooling.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Analyst data plumbing: advanced SQL with joins, window functions and CTEs; querying a warehouse rather than a CSV export; writing a repeatable query instead of one-off edits; and documenting metric definitions so two people compute the same number the same way. Extract, transform and load (ETL) concepts, plus orchestration tools such as Apache Airflow and dbt, are increasingly listed even for analyst roles.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Analysis tooling: Python with pandas and NumPy, or R, for manipulation and numerics; Microsoft Excel is still the most frequently listed tool for this occupation, particularly pivot tables, lookups and modelling; Microsoft Power BI, Tableau, Google Looker Analytics, Alteryx and IBM SPSS cover the visual and statistical layer; SAS and MATLAB appear for heavier statistical work.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Statistics every analyst is expected to hold: distributions and when they mislead, sampling and selection bias, confidence intervals, significance testing, and the difference between a correlation and a causal claim. O*NET lists mathematics among the essential skills for this occupation. Expect an interview question about a metric that moved, and whether the change was real or noise.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 + ESCO skill definitions (CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Experimentation and A/B testing: state the hypothesis, the unit of randomisation, the primary metric and the sample required before starting. The failure mode interviewers probe is stopping a test early because the result looked good and then reporting the peak as the finding. Guardrail metrics exist to catch a primary metric that improved while something else got worse.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Data visualisation and reporting: choose the chart before the tool. Time series take lines, comparisons take bars, distributions take histograms or box plots, relationships take scatter plots; avoid pie charts with more than four slices. O*NET records Tableau, Microsoft Power BI, Google Looker Analytics, QlikView and SAP Crystal Reports for this occupation. Naming one dashboard actually built is enough.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Warehouse and platform layer: Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift and AWS, Apache Hive, Elasticsearch, MongoDB and Amazon DynamoDB appear across the technology records for business intelligence analysts, alongside data modelling tooling such as Informatica and Erwin. The transferable point is dimensional thinking - fact tables, dimension tables and a grain you can state out loud.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Business Intelligence Analysts 15-2051.01 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: The analyst's deliverable is a decision, not a chart. Write the headline first, then the evidence that supports it, then the caveat that limits it. Interviews routinely ask for a technical finding compressed into two sentences for a non-technical stakeholder, so practise dropping detail without dropping the caveat. O*NET lists writing and speaking among the essential skills for this occupation.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Project Management Specialists (O*NET-SOC 13-1082.00) coordinate scope, schedule, budget and people so that a defined piece of work actually lands. O*NET lists the essential skills as active listening, critical thinking, monitoring, writing, active learning, reading comprehension and speaking, with knowledge of administration and management. The graduate bar is structured thinking and visible ownership, not seniority.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: User research and discovery: articulate the user problem before proposing a solution; write non-leading interview questions; run a small study without wasting participants' time; and synthesise findings into themes rather than anecdotes. A credible junior can say what evidence would change their mind and what they would need to collect to get it. Defining the problem precisely is the skill being assessed.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Planning and delivery: a product roadmap that states sequence and rationale; backlog grooming; writing user stories with acceptance criteria; defining what done means; and running a stand-up without letting it degenerate into a status report. Atlassian Jira and Confluence are the trackers named for this occupation. Prioritisation frameworks - RICE, MoSCoW, impact versus effort - are tested through reasoning, not the acronym.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Product metrics: activation, retention, engagement, conversion, and the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator. Choose one primary metric and at most two guardrails. Applying for a role without being able to name the metric you would try to move is a common and avoidable mistake; monitoring and critical thinking are listed by O*NET as essential skills for this occupation.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Stakeholder management: identify who is affected, what each party is optimising for, and how to surface a disagreement before it becomes a blocker. Junior practitioners are expected to escalate early and with a recommendation attached rather than with a problem statement. O*NET records coordination of people and resources as core knowledge for project management specialists.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Market and competitive analysis: define the segment, name the alternatives a user has today including doing nothing, and state the differentiation in one sentence. Being able to read a product's public documentation and pricing page and infer its likely strategy is a standard junior exercise. Segment definition and the do-nothing alternative are the two parts most often skipped.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 (US DOL/ETA, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Wireframing and prototyping: a low-fidelity sketch that makes a flow arguable is worth more than a polished mockup that hides the logic. Figma appears in the technology records for adjacent design work; Microsoft Visio is recorded for process mapping. The assessed skill is whether the artefact exposes an assumption someone can disagree with.

chunks.source: O*NET 31.0, Project Management Specialists 13-1082.00 + 15-2051.01 (CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Analytical tooling a product or project manager is expected to touch: SQL for pulling your own numbers instead of waiting on an analyst, Excel or Google Sheets for modelling and pivots, and a BI tool such as Tableau or Microsoft Power BI for a dashboard. O*NET records spreadsheet, database query and business-intelligence software across both project management and business intelligence occupations.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0) + O*NET technology records
chunks.text: Model deployment is the set of practices that put a trained model behind an interface other software can call: packaging the artefact, versioning it, exposing it as a service, and watching it once live. Containerisation with Docker makes the runtime reproducible, Kubernetes schedules it, and CI/CD automates the path from commit to running service. O*NET records Docker, GitHub, Kubernetes and Jenkins as hot technologies for data-scientist roles.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: A knowledge base for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) should be small, well-defined and chunked by meaning rather than by fixed length: each chunk carries one complete thought, keeps its section title, and carries metadata for attribution. Retrieval quality, not the model, is the usual cause of a RAG system that still produces unsupported answers - noise or too many weakly relevant chunks crowd out the right passage. Prefer a few strongly relevant chunks over many.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: A large language model (LLM) is a language model trained on very large text corpora that generates text by predicting continuation. For a grounded application the relevant engineering concerns are prompt design that separates retrieved context from instructions, an explicit instruction to answer only from the supplied context, a defined behaviour when the context does not contain the answer, and the cost of the tokens each call consumes.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: A vector database stores documents as embedding vectors and retrieves by similarity search rather than by exact term match. The practical consequence is that ranking quality depends entirely on the embedder: a semantic model puts a correct paraphrase near the query, while a purely lexical vector space only rewards shared wording. O*NET lists vector search under the AI skill set for data-scientist roles.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: An A/B test compares two variants on a randomly split population so that the difference in a primary metric can be attributed to the change rather than to pre-existing differences between groups. Prerequisites are a stated hypothesis, a defined randomisation unit, a primary metric fixed in advance, and a sample size calculated before the test starts - not after the results are visible.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Extract, transform and load (ETL) moves data from source systems into a warehouse: extract from the source, transform by cleaning, conforming and joining, then load into a target schema. Modern practice often reverses the middle two steps as ELT, loading raw first and transforming inside the warehouse with a tool such as dbt and an orchestrator such as Apache Airflow. Either way, the contract is a repeatable, documented pipeline rather than manual edits.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: A RESTful API exposes resources over HTTP: a URL identifies the resource, the method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) states the intent, and the status code reports the outcome. Stateless calls, content negotiation and authentication headers are the conventions. The design questions that come up in interviews are versioning, pagination, idempotency of retries, and what the client should do when the dependency is slow or unavailable.

chunks.source: ESCO v1.2.0 skill definitions (European Commission, CC BY 4.0)
chunks.text: Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) automate the path from commit to deployable artefact: on every push the pipeline installs dependencies, runs the test suite, and either blocks the merge or publishes a build. Jenkins CI, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Atlassian Bamboo are the runners O*NET records for this work. The evidence that matters on a graduate CV is a pipeline the candidate configured, and a bad change it stopped.
